sections.title: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
sections.rationale: Beginning with the debate’s definition of rational belief, this section groups the competing accounts of why human cognition can be trusted and the ensuing exchange over evolutionary truth-tracking and theistic reliability.

moveAssignments.rationale: This definition supplies the evidential standard that organizes the later dispute over whether theistic belief is rational rather than merely true or false.
This constructive states the principal theistic inference from reliable minds and an intelligible universe to an intelligent creator.
This move develops the evolutionary reliability challenge in full and distinguishes unguided evolution from a process intended by God to produce rational knowers.
This reply supplies two major structural objections: the separation of atheism from naturalism and the distinction between undermining an alternative and establishing theism.
This move provides the central evolutionary counteraccount, linking broadly accurate representation to the survival costs of systematically false beliefs.
This reply restates the contrast between truth as an intended cognitive function and truth as an intermittent correlate of evolutionary success.
This move completes the exchange by arguing that inaccessible divine reasoning creates an analogous reliability problem for the theistic account.

sections.title: Gratuitous Evil, Theodicy, and Restoration
sections.rationale: This section collects the initial evidential challenge from apparently purposeless suffering, the evil-God comparison, the concession about its significance, and the principal theistic accounts of normativity, afterlife, theodicy, and divine participation in suffering.

moveAssignments.rationale: This constructive introduces the debate’s principal suffering-based challenge by contrasting observed apparently gratuitous evil with the asserted divine attributes.
The evil-God comparison supplies a central probability test for possible reconciliations and develops the initial suffering argument beyond simple inconsistency.
This concession marks suffering as a central point of dispute while serving mainly as a transition into the con side’s substantive replies.
This reply introduces a normative contrast between Christianity’s account of a world that ought to be otherwise and a universe characterized by indifference.
This move adds the afterlife and possible restoration to the temporal frame within which earthly suffering is assessed.
This reply gathers the principal theodicy families and the claim of divine participation in suffering into the con side’s response structure.

sections.title: Salvation Confusion and the Identity of God
sections.rationale: This section connects the critique of disputed salvation conditions with the cumulative case for rational theism and the later contention that generic creator arguments do not by themselves identify an all-powerful, all-loving religious God.

moveAssignments.rationale: This constructive states the salvation-confusion problem through the combination of grave consequences and disagreement about the beliefs required for salvation.
This move develops the salvation critique by connecting hidden or disputed requirements with divine love, human access, and threatened punishment.
This constructive integrates the arguments from rationality, design, and morality into the con side’s cumulative motion-level case.
This reply directly addresses what the cumulative arguments could identify by separating a generic creator from the all-powerful, all-loving God under debate.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning and Evolutionary Accounts of Design
sections.rationale: This section places the cosmic fine-tuning argument alongside the later evolutionary account of apparent biological design, preserving the debate’s distinct but related explanations of ordered and life-permitting features.

moveAssignments.rationale: This constructive supplies the section’s principal design inference from narrow life-permitting physical conditions to intelligent calibration.
This move provides the pro side’s natural explanatory alternative for apparent biological design and locates its significance within changing available evidence.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Evolution, and Divine Goodness
sections.rationale: This section groups the moral argument for God, the evolutionary account of moral intuitions, and the extended exchange over whether goodness is independent of God, arbitrarily commanded, or grounded in the divine nature.

moveAssignments.rationale: This constructive states the principal moral argument by presenting objective moral obligation as requiring an explanation grounded in God.
This reply supplies an evolutionary account of care, sacrifice, moral intuition, and the emotional force of religious narratives.
This move introduces the section’s central dilemma concerning whether goodness exists independently of God or depends on divine command.
This reply adds the historical claim that biblical teaching about divine image-bearing helped furnish the moral standards used in the critique.
This move states the principal divine-nature response by grounding objective goodness in God rather than in an external standard or arbitrary command.
This reply completes the exchange by arguing that identifying God with goodness restates rather than removes the underlying dilemma.

bridgeMappings.rationale: The retained evidence spans the governing rationality standard, the principal challenges from suffering and salvation confusion, and the later argument about whether a creator can be identified with the God specified by the motion.

These moves preserve the structural comparison between evil and epistemic confusion on one side and the cumulative positive case on the other, including the dispute over what kind of deity that case could establish.

The mapping retains the full suffering exchange: apparently gratuitous evil, the evil-God comparison, the concession about its centrality, normative and afterlife replies, recognized theodicies, and the later divine-identity consequence.
Both retained moves are assigned together because they state and develop the same salvation-confusion line concerning severe consequences, disputed requirements, limited access, and divine love.

The retained evidence is distributed across the three relevant explanatory disputes: cognitive reliability, apparent design, and morality. Together those sections preserve the evolutionary and alternative-explanation material associated with this bridge.
The mapping retains the three constructive strands from reason, design, and morality as well as the move that explicitly combines them into the con side’s cumulative case concerning rational belief.

These retained moves preserve every component of the cumulative structure: reason, fine-tuning, morality, their explicit combination, and the concession and replies intended to keep suffering within the same overall evidential comparison.

All retained evidence for this bridge is grouped in the rationality section, including the unguided-evolution challenge, the guided-evolution contrast, and the successive evolutionary and parity-based replies.

The mapping places the fine-tuning constructive and the evolutionary account of apparent design in the design section while retaining the later creator-identity reply in the section addressing what such arguments could establish.

The morality section retains the objective-morality constructive, evolutionary alternative, divine-command dilemma, historical biblical account, divine-nature response, and final restatement objection as one complete topical exchange.
